Before we open the reading, I want to clear up the mistake that appears in almost every first essay in this course. Students write that a country signed a treaty and is therefore bound by it. That is not how it works. There are three different moments, and they are often years apart. First, the text is adopted, which means the negotiators agree on the words. Second, it is signed, which shows that a state supports the text. And third, it is ratified, usually after a parliament approves it. Only the third moment creates a legal obligation for that state. And even then, many treaties only enter into force after a minimum number of ratifications. So when you read a headline that says a treaty was signed today, ask yourself one question: signed, or ratified? The answer changes the whole article.

Every time a government threatens to leave an international agreement, our listeners send us the same question: can a country just walk out? The short answer is yes, but not overnight. Most treaties contain their own exit rules, and those rules are usually slower than politicians would like. A written notice has to be sent, and the withdrawal only takes effect after a waiting period, often one year. During that year, the country is still a party, and it is still expected to comply with every provision. Some agreements go further and say that no one can withdraw during the first few years after the treaty enters into force. So when you hear that a country has left an agreement, check the date the notice was given. The country may still be bound for months.
